title: Stasimon 2 (lines 549–588)

teacherSummary.text: The Chorus sings that when the gods shake a house, ruin passes from generation to generation, as in the house of Labdacus. Zeus' power never sleeps, and hope can deceive until the ground burns underfoot.

Age after age describes the curse moving through generations of mortals, each forced to drain the cup. Untouched by Time describes Zeus, who stands outside that process. The contrast shows human beings caught in time and suffering, while the divine power that punishes excess is permanent and beyond reach.

The Ode on Man celebrated human daring and skill, limited only by death and by the need to honour law and the gods. This ode is darker: humans are victims of inherited curses and deceptive hope, and Zeus's power crushes all excess. Together the odes show human greatness and human helplessness side by side.

satQuestions.passage:
Thrice blest are they who never tasted pain!
If once the curse of Heaven attaint a race,
The infection lingers on and speeds apace,
Age after age, and each the cup must drain.
So when Etesian blasts from Thrace downpour
Sweep o’er the blackening main and whirl to land
From Ocean’s cavernous depths his ooze and sand,
Billow on billow thunders on the shore.
On the Labdacidae I see descending
Woe upon woe; from days of old some god
Laid on the race a malison, and his rod
Scourges each age with sorrows never ending.
The light that dawned upon its last born son
Is vanished, and the bloody axe of Fate
Has felled the goodly tree that blossomed late.
O Oedipus, by reckless pride undone!

anchorPassages.note: Choral wisdom on measure: pride and false hope burn like ash underfoot.
anchorPassages.text:
Thy might, O Zeus, what mortal power can quell?
Not sleep that lays all else beneath its spell,
Nor moons that never tire: untouched by Time,
Throned in the dazzling light
That crowns Olympus’ height,
Thou reignest King, omnipotent, sublime.
Past, present, and to be,
All bow to thy decree,
All that exceeds the mean by Fate
Is punished, Love or Hate.
Hope flits about on never-wearying wings;
Profit to some, to some light loves she brings,
But no man knoweth how her gifts may turn,
Till ’neath his feet the treacherous ashes burn.
Sure ’twas a sage inspired that spake this word;
If evil good appear
To any, Fate is near;
And brief the respite from her flaming sword.

Read closely: “Hope flits about on never-wearying wings; Profit to some, to some light loves she brings, But no man knoweth how her gifts may turn, Till ’neath his feet the treacherous ashes burn.” (Chorus, lines 575–578).
analysis.weDoWords: “Never-wearying wings”, “gifts” and “treacherous ashes” stand out in lines 575–578. Hope is pictured as a restless bird and as ground that hides fire, so the elders warn that hope can lead a person into ruin. “No man knoweth how her gifts may turn” keeps the danger uncertain until the ashes burn.

Today's words: blest — made happy or fortunate; attaint — to stain a family with a curse or disgrace; malison — a curse upon a person or family; scourges — punishes severely, as with a whip; omnipotent — having unlimited power; forlorn — pitifully alone and unhappy.

The house of Labdacus is the family of Laius, Oedipus and his children. The ode places Antigone inside an inherited curse, yet her choice is her own: the play balances fate and responsibility. Imagery: Hope “flits about on never-wearying wings” until the ground burns, so hope itself becomes a treacherous landscape underfoot. Foreshadowing: Ruin that “lingers on and speeds apace” from age to age points forward to the deaths still to come in Creon’s house as well as Oedipus’s. Watch for burial and the unburied body: The curse-song keeps the family’s past graves in view, while Polyneices’s present lack of a grave is the fresh wound the curse is feeding on.

Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

items.text: Retell the most important events of “Stasimon 2 (lines 549–588)” in order, one sentence for each event.
items.lookFor: The Chorus sings that when the gods shake a house, ruin passes from generation to generation, as in the house of Labdacus. Zeus' power never sleeps, and hope can deceive until the ground burns underfoot.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: The Chorus sings that when the gods shake a house, ruin passes from generation to generation, as in the house of Labdacus. Zeus' power never sleeps, and hope can deceive until the ground burns underfoot.

items.text: Why does the Chorus speak of hope right after Antigone's sentence?
items.lookFor: Hope can deceive a person as ruin approaches, citing the ode’s wording.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The ode turns from the sentence just passed to Hope that “flits about on never-wearying wings” and may hide “treacherous ashes” (lines 575–578). The elders suggest that hope can deceive a person just as ruin approaches, a warning that hangs over Creon as well as over the doomed house.

items.text: What does “Stasimon 2 (lines 549–588)” suggest about the curse on the house? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: The ode places Antigone inside an inherited curse, yet her choice is her own: the play balances fate and responsibility.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The ode places Antigone inside an inherited curse, yet her choice is her own: the play balances fate and responsibility. Evidence to accept: “Thrice blest are they who never tasted pain” (Stasimon 2, line 549): Chorus, line 549. Credit any reading that quotes the text and explains it.

items.text: Find one example of theme in “Stasimon 2 (lines 549–588)”. What does it reveal about the curse on the house that a plain statement would not?

items.text: How does the imagery in “Stasimon 2 (lines 549–588)” shape what we understand about the curse on the house?

items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The ode places Antigone inside an inherited curse, yet her choice is her own: the play balances fate and responsibility. Useful evidence: “Thrice blest are they who never tasted pain” (Stasimon 2, line 549): Chorus, line 549. On imagery: Hope “flits about on never-wearying wings” until the ground burns, so hope itself becomes a treacherous landscape underfoot. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.
